title: Is artificial intelligence improving the audit process?
author: Anastassia Fedyk · James Hodson · Natalya Khimich · Tatiana Fedyk

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster with large-scale evidence from auditing, an adjacent professional-services context: AI investment is associated with improved quality and productivity alongside delayed workforce reductions concentrated among junior staff. This strengthens the cluster’s account of immediate gains and entry-level competence-pipeline risks, although it is not direct evidence about legal workflows or lawyer replacement.
qs: Moreover, we find preliminary evidence that improved audit quality is accompanied by a move towards a leaner process: as audit firms invest in AI, they are able to lower the fees they charge while reducing their audit workforces and showing increased productivity, as measured by total fees per employee.

A one- standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the past three years predicts a decrease of 5.7% in the number of junior accounting employees three years later and an even larger decrease of 11.8% four years later.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study extends the cluster with large-scale, observational evidence from auditing: AI adoption is associated with delayed workforce reductions concentrated among juniors, while interviews identify trained human capital, scaling and deployment as the principal implementation barriers. This materially reinforces the cluster’s claims about operating-model redesign and junior-work risks, although it does not directly establish effects in legal practice or address verification.
qs: A one- standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the past three years predicts a decrease of 5.7% in the number of junior accounting employees three years later and an even larger decrease of 11.8% four years later.

kp.k: Resume data measure actual AI hiring in auditing
kp.d: The study examines 2010–2019 using more than 310,000 employee profiles from 36 large U.S. public accounting firms, combining Cognism resumes with Audit Analytics. Its main AI-investment measure is the change over three years in the proportion of employees identified as AI workers through job records, publications, patents or awards. The sample requires at least 100 matched employees and at least one AI worker during the period. This is evidence about accounting and auditing, rather than a direct study of legal services.
qs: Our sample spans 2010–2019, covers the 36 largest U.S. public accounting firms with at least 100 employees, and analyzes more than 310,000 employee profiles.
The classification is performed at the level of each individual job record of each worker.
We find that Cognism covers approximately 86% of public accounting employees

kp.k: AI investment is associated with fewer restatements
kp.d: The main restatement analysis covers 20,010 issuer-year observations for 2010–2017, allowing time for subsequent restatements to emerge. With client controls and industry and year fixed effects, the authors report that a one-standard-deviation increase in the auditor’s AI-worker share over the preceding three years is associated with reductions of 5% in restatement likelihood, 1.4% in material restatements, 1.9% in revenue-and-accrual restatements and 0.3% in restatement-related SEC investigations. These are the paper’s stated percentage descriptions; Table 4 reports corresponding indicator-outcome OLS coefficients of −0.050, −0.014, −0.019 and −0.003.
qs: a one-standard-deviation increase in an audit firm’s share of AI employees over the course of the prior three years is associated with a 5% reduction in the likelihood of restatements, a 1.4% reduction in the likelihood of material restatements, a 1.9% reduction in the likelihood of restatements related to accrual and revenue recognition, and a 0.3% reduction in the likelihood of restatements related to SEC investigations.
Standard errors are clustered by issuer.

kp.k: Quality associations are specific, not universal
kp.d: Restatement associations are present in both Big Four and non-Big Four firms and are stronger in the later 2014–2017 period. They remain after accounting for software-engineering and general data-analysis skills. However, the authors report no significant association between AI adoption and accrual measures, audit-report lag, or Type 1 and Type 2 going-concern errors. Their evidence therefore supports particular audit-quality outcomes rather than improvement across every measure.
qs: Overall, the results are very consistent across the two subsamples.
Importantly, the effect of AI remains almost unchanged when we add Data Analysis and Software Engineering
Overall, we do not find evidence of a significant association between the adoption of AI and accruals.
AI is not associated with differences in the time lag between the fiscal year end and the audit report or with the incidence of Type 1 or Type 2 errors in going concern opinions.

kp.k: Small centralized AI teams support firm-wide deployment
kp.d: AI workers increased from 0.08% of the sampled workforce in 2010 to 0.39% in 2018 and 0.37% in 2019. More than half were concentrated in New York, California, Washington D.C., Illinois and Texas. Interviews describe centralized development and top-down implementation, with Big Four firms combining internal development and external purchases, and smaller firms relying more on external solutions and AICPA partnerships. Firm-wide AI investment has stronger restatement associations than local-office investment.
qs: AI tools used in audit are predominately developed in centralized hubs and implemented as top-down standard procedures.
By contrast, smaller firms rely more on external solutions and often coordinate and co- invest by partnering with AICPA.
when we control for firm- wide adoption of AI, the coefficient estimates on ΔAI_office_level(−3,0)i,t become statistically insignificant in all but one specification.

kp.k: Partners prioritize quality and redirect human attention
kp.d: Seventeen interviews conducted between November 2021 and January 2022 involved partners and technology leaders from the eight largest U.S. accounting firms: nine Big Four and eight non-Big Four participants. They describe applications in anomaly and fraud detection, revenue analysis, risk assessment, anti-money laundering, contract and lease review, and analysis of public databases. Interviewees emphasize audit quality first, with automation releasing auditors from routine work to focus on problematic areas and more complex tasks.
qs: Interviews took place over the three-month period from November 2021 to January 2022.
Quality is a must. Our main goal is improved quality, and if we are lucky, we are more efficient.

AI enables the implementation of new audit models, directs auditors to the areas that are likely to be most problematic, and frees human auditors from routine jobs, allowing them to concentrate on more important tasks.
labor effects concentrate on removing lower-level tasks and asking people to take on more complex tasks and/or handle larger volume of tasks.

kp.k: Deployment requires training and internal adoption incentives
kp.d: Interviewees identify skilled human capital, scaling and deployment as major implementation constraints. Firms reportedly make 30–40 AI-based tools available, with varying requirements by engagement, and expect partners to use them on at least 2–3 clients, particularly new and large clients. Adoption is incorporated into performance assessment. One interviewee describes a decision to digitally upskill all 60K employees, from first-year staff to partners; this is an individual firm account, not a sector-wide training count.
qs: Firms have up to 30– 40 AI-based tools that are available for auditors’ practical use
partners are expected to use these tools on at least 2–3 clients
Developing new tools is relatively easy, it’s scaling and deploying that takes the most effort.
we strategically decided to digitally upskill all 60K employees—from first years to partners.

kp.k: Auditor investment matters more than client AI investment
kp.d: Using parallel resume-based measures for audit clients, the authors find negligible quality associations for clients’ AI investment while auditors’ AI coefficients remain essentially unchanged. Partners report that clients expect advanced technology and lower audit fees but generally rely on auditors to supply audit-specific AI. These observations distinguish the provider’s technological investment from the buyer’s own AI adoption.
qs: While clients’ AI has a negligible effect on audit quality, the effect of auditors’ AI is virtually unchanged from that in Table 4
Clients almost never invest in AI for audit purposes; they don’t understand audit well enough to make such moves. Auditors do.

kp.k: Benefits vary with client age and engagement context
kp.d: The authors predict greater benefits where accumulated data or transaction patterns suit AI. They report restatement reductions of 4.3% for the youngest client-age tercile and 6.5% for the oldest. New-client interaction estimates are negative across restatement outcomes but significant only for material restatements; retail-specific evidence is significant for revenue-and-accrual restatements. These tests offer qualified support for the proposed mechanisms rather than uniformly significant subgroup differences.
qs: a one-standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers decreases the probability of a restatement by 4.3% among the youngest tercile of client firms and by 6.5% among the oldest tercile of client firms.
the coefficients on ΔAIi, t × NewClienti, t are negative for all restatement variables and significant for material restatements.
significant for revenue and accruals restatements.

kp.k: Audit fees decline gradually following AI investment
kp.d: A one-standard-deviation increase in AI-worker share over the prior three years predicts audit-fee reductions of 0.9%, 1.5% and 2.1% after one, two and three years, respectively, controlling for initial fees and other client characteristics. The authors treat this as preliminary efficiency evidence. Interviews reveal competing pressures: clients expect savings to reduce prices, whereas auditors emphasize upfront investment costs and delayed efficiency gains. The paper explicitly notes that efficiency gains need not automatically be passed through.
qs: a one-standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the previous three years predicts a 0.9% reduction in per-audit fees in the following year.
a one-standard deviation increase in the share of AI employees over the previous three years forecasts a 1.5% (2.1%) reduction in log per-audit fees after two (three) years.
even if audit efficiency increases with AI adoption, audit firms might not pass their savings on to clients.

kp.k: Delayed employment reductions concentrate among junior accounting staff
kp.d: Firm-level regressions associate a one-standard-deviation rise in AI-worker share over the previous three years with 3.6% fewer accounting employees after three years and 7.1% after four years; first- and second-year results are not significant. Junior reductions are 5.7% and 11.8% at three and four years, with no significant displacement at middle or senior levels. Accounting employment combines audit and tax because some job records span both. These conditional firm-level findings coexist with growth in the sampled firms’ total workforce over 2010–2019.
qs: a one-standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the past three years translates into a decrease of 3.6% in accounting employees three years later and an even greater drop of 7.1% four years out.
the lack of significant results in the first and second years indicates that the reduction in human labor due to AI takes time to implement.
We find a significant displacement effect of AI adoption on the labor force only at the junior level.

A one- standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the past three years predicts a decrease of 5.7% in the number of junior accounting employees three years later and an even larger decrease of 11.8% four years later.

kp.k: Efficiency gains may distribute benefits unequally
kp.d: The authors find preliminary evidence of higher fees per accounting employee alongside lower fees and reduced staffing. They interpret this as a leaner audit process but caution that benefits may accrue unevenly: partners gain from quality, efficiency and personnel-cost reductions, while juniors face delayed displacement. This is the authors’ interpretation of audit-sector evidence, not a demonstrated conclusion about lawyers or legal-market staffing.
qs: While our results about increased efficiency are more preliminary than our main findings on audit quality, they provide an important complementary perspective to the quality angle.
our findings on the labor impacts of AI caution that the gains from new technologies may not be distributed equally across the population.

While partners of audit firms benefit from increased product quality, greater efficiency, and reductions in personnel costs, junior employees may suffer from the displacement we observe several years after AI investments.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Fedyk, Hodson, Khimich and Fedyk claim that AI investment improves audit quality, lowers audit fees and eventually reduces accounting employment, particularly among junior employees.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of auditing, not a study of legal services. The authors formulate and test three predictions: improved quality, improved efficiency and reduced employment. For a one-standard-deviation increase in the share of AI workers over the preceding three years, they report reductions in restatement likelihood of 5.0%, material restatements of 1.4%, revenue/accrual-related restatements of 1.9% and restatement-related SEC involvement of 0.3%. These are the authors' percentage descriptions; Table 4's coefficients on binary outcomes are −0.050, −0.014, −0.019 and −0.003, respectively, corresponding to percentage-point changes in the linear probability specification. They report approximately 0.9%, 1.5% and 2.1% lower audit fees one, two and three years ahead. Their employment regressions associate AI investment with 3.6% and 7.1% lower accounting employment growth over three and four years, described in the text as workforce reductions. Junior-level estimates are 5.7% and 11.8%; mid-tier and senior displacement estimates are not statistically significant. The authors also claim increased fees per accounting employee as evidence of productivity gains, while describing the efficiency findings as preliminary.

pts.k: Interviewed audit partners describe AI as automating routine analysis and redirecting auditors toward higher-risk and more complex work; the authors identify centralized deployment as the predominant organizational model.
pts.d: Partners and national technology leaders report applications in anomaly and fraud detection, revenue analysis, risk assessment, anti-money-laundering work, contract and lease processing, and analysis of large public databases. They describe quality as the primary objective and efficiency as secondary. Human auditors remain involved, but routine tasks are removed and individual workloads can increase. According to interviewees, AI tools are developed in central hubs and rolled out through top-down procedures and performance incentives. Big Four firms combine internal development with external purchases; smaller firms rely more on external solutions and collaboration through AICPA. The authors report that firm-wide AI employment measures explain quality improvements more strongly than office-level measures and that auditors' AI investment, rather than clients' investment, accounts for the restatement association.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on resume-based measures of AI employment, linked audit outcomes and regression analyses, supplemented by 17 semi-structured interviews.
pts.d: The empirical dataset covers more than 310,000 employee profiles at 36 large U.S. public accounting firms during 2010–2019, including Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC and 32 non-Big Four firms. Sample inclusion requires at least 100 matched employees and at least one identified AI worker during the sample period; the authors report robustness to dropping the latter restriction. Cognism resumes are linked to Audit Analytics, with coverage validated against Accounting Today employment counts at approximately 86%. AI investment is proxied by changes in the share of employees whose job records, publications, patents or awards indicate AI activity, rather than directly measured spending or engagement-level usage. Main quality regressions use 20,010 issuer-year observations, client characteristics, industry and year fixed effects, and issuer-clustered standard errors. Additional analyses compare periods and firm types, control for general software-engineering and data-analysis skills, and distinguish auditor, client and office-level AI. Fee regressions additionally control for initial fees. Employment regressions use firm-level workforce growth, year fixed effects, Big Four status and total fees. Interviews with partners and national technology leaders from the eight largest firms provide reported experience concerning mechanisms and implementation. The quantitative evidence is observational association, although the authors also use causal language in stating their conclusions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The study concerns AI adoption in 2010–2019, with quality associations strengthening later in that period and employment effects appearing only after several years.
pts.d: The main investment measure is the change in AI-worker share over the prior three years. Main restatement regressions cover fiscal years 2010–2017 to allow subsequent discovery and reporting through 2019. Quality associations are stronger in 2014–2017 than in 2010–2013. Fee reductions are estimated one to three years ahead; accounting employment effects are not significant after one or two years but appear after three and four. Interviews were conducted from November 2021 to January 2022; interviewees generally date investment beginnings to around 2010–2012, with some suggesting a plateau in the preceding one or two years. Deployment depends especially on training and skilled human capital. Partners distinguish the relative ease of tool development from the difficulty of scaling adoption. The authors expect greater benefits where extensive data and repeat transactions are available. Their subgroup analyses find stronger results for older clients; additional new-client benefits are statistically significant for material restatements, and additional retail benefits for revenue/accrual restatements. These are not claims about generative AI or a forecast of full professional replacement. The study also reports no significant associations with accrual-based quality measures, audit-report lag or going-concern errors.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify uneven consequences: audit firms and partners gain quality and efficiency benefits, clients receive lower fees, and junior accounting staff bear the observed displacement.
pts.d: Quality associations occur in both Big Four and non-Big Four audit firms; these firms are studied as accounting providers, not as entrants into legal services. The employment outcome combines audit and tax personnel because some job descriptions span both functions; the authors report stronger results when restricted to audit-only titles. The junior category includes staff, assistants, associates, analysts and senior accountants/auditors, while managers and partners fall into separate categories without statistically significant displacement. Remaining staff are expected to undertake more complex tasks or serve greater volumes of work, and personnel across seniority levels face upskilling requirements. Corporate audit clients expect advanced technology and lower fees, although partners emphasize upfront investment costs and delayed efficiency gains. Older clients, new engagements and retail clients are identified as particularly promising settings, subject to the outcome-specific qualifications above. The findings concern differences in firm-level employment growth, not an observed aggregate collapse in accounting employment: the sample's overall workforce grew substantially during the period. The authors do not quantify consequences for lawyers or legal markets.
